events.text: Day 1 begins.

Morning, everyone. I'll go first since I'm eager to hear how people read each other before we lock anything in.

My own read this early is thin, but I'll say what I have. I don't know Kenji (p5) at all, and I think that's exactly the problem with him — he's given us nothing to work with while everyone else is putting out actual opinions. In a nine-player game with only two of us on the other side, silence is expensive. A villager with a plan should be able to name who they'd vote for and why. Kenji hasn't named a single player, and I'd rather cut someone loose now than spend three more days guessing.

Before we vote, though, I want to hear the rest of you. Leo (p7), you've been around and you seem thoughtful — what is your read on the group so far, and who do you think has been most or least convincing? I'd rather have honest disagreement here than a false consensus we all regret tonight.

I'll also add: I don't think anyone should be eliminated on pure vibes just because they're quiet. If Kenji has something to say, he still has his turns to say it, and if the answer is that he's hiding, then that settles it. But I want to know what the rest of you think before I commit my vote, and I won't be voting for anyone whose case is just "they seemed nervous to me."

Omar, thanks for yielding. I think your concern about Kenji is fair, but I don't want to treat silence as guilt this early — quiet villagers get mislynched all the time on day one, and your own message says you don't want a vibes-only elimination. So I'd rather pressure Kenji for content than commit to him now.

Kenji, your name is on the table. I need you to name one living player you'd vote for and one player you currently trust, each with a concrete reason. If you can't do that, I'll be much more willing to vote you. I'm not asking for a perfect read, just evidence you're actually solving.

On the rest: I don't have a strong scumread yet. Arjun, Zara, Isha, Felix, and Lucia haven't given me enough to judge. Elena too. Omar's push is coherent, but I'm watching whether he locks onto Kenji too fast if Kenji gives a reasonable answer. I won't vote on nervousness alone.

Leo, you asked for a concrete answer, so here it is. My current vote is Omar (p8). His whole case against me is that I haven't named anyone, which is fair, and I'm happy to answer that now. But he opened day one by calling for a lynch on the quiet player, the kind of vibes-based push he says he won't make. He also said he won't vote on nervousness, then cited my silence as the reason to cut me loose. I want him to explain that contradiction.

On trust, I currently trust Leo (p7). He asked for evidence instead of calling for a quick lynch, and he gave me a clear test rather than a verdict. I'd like everyone held to that standard. I don't have a strong read on Arjun, Zara, Isha, Felix, Elena, or Lucia yet, since most of them have been quiet. I think that's where we are on day one, and I'd rather hear a few more real positions before anyone's vote gets locked in.

Omar, you said silence is expensive. Beyond the fact that I haven't named a target yet, what specifically did I say or do that makes you think I'm hiding?

Kenji, direct answer: I named you because you had produced zero content — no name, no trust, no target — while six other players have spoken and I had to pick someone. That is all I had. I didn't claim you were hiding a role; I claimed you were silent, and I said in the same breath that silence isn't guilt and that I wouldn't vote on nervousness. You're now calling that a contradiction, but the contradiction is mine to own and I'd rather own it than pretend I had a hidden tell I didn't.

That said, note what your answer actually did: it produced no new information about anyone except me. You voted for me because I spoke against you, and you trusted Leo because Leo set a test you could pass by answering a question I asked you. If that's the standard — "name someone to prove you're solving" — then it applies to everyone who hasn't spoken, not just me. Zara, Isha, Felix, Elena, and Arjun have all been quiet so far. If Kenji's standard is good enough to justify his vote on me, it's good enough to justify mine on the players who have given us literally nothing.

So let me be explicit and narrow my case rather than broaden it. I'm no longer asking anyone to lynch Kenji for silence; if he answers with a real read, that's the answer to my concern. But my vote today goes to Zara, who has said nothing at all — not a read, not a question, not even a token opinion. Not because she's quiet in the way Kenji was, but because Kenji has now demonstrated that quietness is not evidence of anything, and the only people who have earned scrutiny are the ones still refusing to engage. Leo, you asked us to avoid vibes-only eliminations, and I agree — so give me a reason for Zara beyond quiet, or tell me who you'd rather test, and I'll take a real answer over a comfortable one.

One more thing for the record: I have no information on anyone's role. Neither does anyone else. Anyone telling you otherwise today is selling something.

Omar, I’m here, and your vote on me is exactly the vibes-only elimination you said you'd avoid. You admit Kenji’s silence wasn’t evidence; then you move your vote to me because I “said nothing at all.” But at the moment you posted, Arjun, Isha, Felix, Elena, and Lucia were equally silent. You singled me out without explaining what distinguishes my silence from theirs. That’s not a narrower case; it’s the same case with a different name.

I don’t accept “quiet equals hiding” on day one. I’ve been reading the exchange: your initial push on Kenji was thin, Kenji answered it, and then you pivoted to me rather than re-evaluate. That pivot looks more like seeking a safe target than solving. If you want scrutiny on silence, apply it consistently and explain why I’m your pick over the other four equally silent players.

I’m not locking a vote yet. I want real content from the quiet players, including me. But Omar, you need to answer this directly: what concrete behavior separates me from Arjun, Isha, Felix, Elena, and Lucia in your case, or are you voting me only because I’m the name you happened to say? I’m yielding to you for that answer.

Zara, direct answer: there is no concrete behavioral difference between your silence and Arjun's, Isha's, Felix's, Elena's, and Lucia's. I named you because I had to name someone and you were the most recent name in front of me, not because you did anything the others didn't. You called that correctly, and I'm not going to dress it up. My vote on you today is withdrawn — you get a pass from me, and I'd ask the rest of the table to hold me to that.

But if we hold everyone to Leo's standard, we have to hold Leo to it too, and so far he hasn't. Leo set the test: name a target, name a trust, give reasons, prove you're solving. Leo himself has done none of those things. He hasn't named a single player he'd vote for, hasn't said who he trusts, and hasn't given a read on anyone in this game — not me, not Kenji, not Zara, not Arjun, Isha, Felix, Elena, or Lucia. He's run the process without ever putting his own hand in it. That's not humility, that's insulation: every question he asks is a question that someone else has to answer, and if nobody names him, the questioner sails through the day without a single person having to defend him.

I want to be precise so this isn't another vibes push. I'm not saying Leo is hiding a role. I'm saying that a standard of "show me you have a position" is either applied to everyone or to nobody, and right now it is only being applied downward. Kenji produced a name, a trust, and a reason, and was put under a microscope for it. Leo has produced nothing and is being treated as the neutral arbiter of that microscope. I want to know what Leo's vote is and who he trusts, with reasons, exactly as he demanded of Kenji — and I want him to answer before the vote is locked, because if his answer is better than mine, I'll take it.

One more thing for the record, and it applies to me as much as anyone: nobody in this game knows anyone's role. If Leo, or anyone else, is about to claim a tell or a pattern that only they can see, that's the thing to be most suspicious of today, including from me.

Omar, fair hit. You’re right that I pushed a standard — name a target, name a trust, give reasons — and then didn’t apply it to myself. So here is my hand on the table.

I currently trust Zara most. She directly challenged your pivot to her and forced you to admit there was no concrete difference between her silence and several others. That was a real position, not process for its own sake.

My current suspicion is Arjun (p2). Not because silence alone is guilt — I meant it when I said quiet villagers get mislynched — but because Arjun has had the same opportunity as everyone else and has produced no read, no question, no vote pressure, and no stated trust. That is still thin on day one, and I will reassess the moment he gives real content. But it is a narrower case than “he was quiet”: it is “he has been present in the player list while the rest of us have made claims and he has not joined the solving at all.”

Arjun, direct question: name one living player you would vote for today and one living player you currently trust, each with a concrete reason. If your answer is real, I will treat it seriously and may move. If it is evasive or absent, my vote will go to you. I’m not asking for a perfect read — I’m asking for evidence you’re actually playing this day rather than waiting for the table to make a mistake.

I also want Isha, Felix, Elena, and Lucia to hear the same standard, but I’m directing it at Arjun because he is my current target. Omar, I’ll say this plainly: I don’t think your withdrawal on Zara clears you, but it was better than doubling down. Keep giving me reasons to read you as town.

Leo, my current vote would be Omar. He opened by treating Kenji’s lack of content as grounds to cut him loose before Kenji had spoken, then shifted the same reasoning to Zara without distinguishing her from the other silent players. He withdrew when challenged, which is better than doubling down, but the repeated arbitrary pressure is my strongest concern so far. He also claimed six others had spoken when the record shows only him, you, and Kenji had spoken at that point.

I currently trust Zara most, though only weakly: she identified the inconsistency in Omar’s pivot and pressed him to explain it rather than simply accepting his target.

Leo, your case on me sounds like the same silence argument you cautioned against. What makes my lack of a statement before this turn different from the other players who haven’t spoken yet?

Arjun, thanks for yielding. The honest answer is: there was no clean behavioral difference between you and Isha, Felix, Elena, or Lucia at the time I named you. You hadn’t spoken. I singled you out because you were my current pressure point after Omar’s withdrawal, and that is not a good enough case. You have now given a target, a trust, and reasons, so you satisfy the test I set. I withdraw my suspicion of you for today.

Updated reads: Zara’s challenge to Omar was a real position and looks towny. Kenji answered under pressure with a concrete vote and trust, so I’m off him for now. Omar’s pivot to Zara was bad — he admitted there was no behavioral difference and withdrew, which is better than doubling down, but I’m not clearing him just for that. Arjun’s answer is acceptable. My remaining suspicion is on the players who still haven’t joined the solving at all: Isha, Felix, Elena, and Lucia. But I won’t repeat Omar’s mistake of picking one silent name by convenience.

Isha, you’re the next name I want to hear from. Name one living player you would vote for today and one living player you currently trust, each with a concrete reason. Also answer specifically: do you read Omar’s pivot to Zara and immediate withdrawal as scummy, clumsy town, or something else? I’m yielding to you for that answer.

Leo, answering your questions in order. My vote today would be Omar (p8). My current trust, weakly, is Zara — her challenge to Omar was the only moment so far where someone forced a concrete admission out of another player, and she did it without manufacturing a target first. Kenji's answer under pressure was also acceptable: he named a vote and a trust with reasons when asked, which is more than most of us have done.

On your specific question about Omar's pivot to Zara and immediate withdrawal: I read it as clumsy town rather than deliberate scum hunting. Here's why. A mafia player who names an arbitrary target and gets called on it can just hold position or deflect — withdrawing and explicitly admitting "there is no behavioral difference, I named you by convenience" is costly and uncomfortable, and Omar did it in full view. That responsiveness is worth something. But it's worth less than Omar seems to think, because the underlying problem is unchanged: he has now applied pressure to two different players on reasoning he himself disowned minutes later. I don't think that pattern makes him mafia, but it means his reads carry no weight with me today, and when someone's judgment is that unreliable, voting them is a defensible way to remove noise from the table.

There's one thing Omar said that bothers me more than the pivots, and I want to put it on the record. Twice now he has declared that "nobody in this game knows anyone's role" and that anyone claiming a tell or information today is "selling something." I understand the surface appeal — it sounds humble and even-handed. But think about what that framing actually does: it pre-discredits any player who comes forward with real information, before anyone has even tried. On a day where nobody has evidence, the honest position is "we have nothing yet, so let's build reads carefully," not "anyone who claims to know something is a liar." That's not neutrality; it's poisoning the well in advance. I'd apply the same skepticism to anyone else who does it, including myself.

So my position is this: I'm not voting Omar because he's quiet, nervous, or arbitrary — I'm voting him because his one genuine contribution this day has been a cycle of pressure, retraction, and pre-emptive dismissal of information claims, and the table has rewarded that with attention while the rest of us scramble to pass tests he invented. If he gives me a better reason to read him as town than "I withdrew, didn't I," I'll move.

Omar, direct question: when you said anyone claiming a tell or information today is "selling something" — did you intend that to apply to a genuine role claim made in good faith later today or tonight? If yes, why should the table discount real information on your say-so? If no, what did that line actually accomplish besides making people afraid to speak up?

Omar, you asked why I was voting you, and I'm still voting for you. Your case has moved from me, to Zara, to a withdrawal, and your line that anyone claiming information today is selling something is the part I most want the table to examine. Isha raised the same point, and I agree: a good-faith claim should be weighed on its merits, not discounted in advance on your say-so. I'm not asking anyone to believe an unverified claim today, but dismissing claims before they are made is not neutral.

On reads: Zara's challenge to you was the strongest content so far, and I trust her for now. Arjun answered Leo's test with a target and a trust, and I'll accept that answer. Leo's reasoning has been consistent, and he has asked for a clear position from everyone else, so I'd like him to keep his own vote visible as the day goes on.

Felix, you're one of the players who has not put out a read yet. Name one living player you would vote for today and one living player you currently trust, each with a concrete reason. I'm not asking you to be right, only to show a position, which is the same test everyone else has been held to.

Kenji, here is my response to your test.

My current trust is Zara (p3). Her pushback against Omar was direct, grounded, and caught an arbitrary pivot cleanly. She didn't panic or overreach; she forced an honest retraction, which reads as genuine town problem-solving.

My primary suspicion and current vote, however, is Isha (p4). 

Isha explicitly stated that she reads Omar’s pivot and retraction as "clumsy town rather than deliberate scum hunting," yet in the same breath kept her vote on him because "voting them is a defensible way to remove noise from the table." Eliminating a player you actively lean toward being town just because their play is erratic or noisy is a classic anti-town line of thinking. It provides a convenient, low-accountability vehicle for a Day 1 mislynch that mafia can easily hide behind.

Additionally, since this game began directly on Day 1 without a Night 0, nobody has investigative results yet. Omar’s blanket remark that nobody knows anyone's role was certainly poorly phrased, but framing it as a sinister plot to suppress future power-role claims felt like an over-engineered justification to push a player Isha already characterized as town.

Isha, how do you justify voting to eliminate someone you explicitly read as clumsy town over searching for mafia, especially when Day 1 mislynches are so costly for town?

Felix, you asked how I justify voting to eliminate someone I read as clumsy town, so here is the direct answer.

On Day 1, with zero information, every uneliminated player carries the same baseline risk. When that's true, the tiebreaker isn't "who is most likely mafia" — nobody knows — it's "whose continued presence costs the table the most." Omar hasn't produced a single read that survived his own retraction of it. He pressured Kenji on reasoning he disowned, moved to Zara on reasoning he disowned, and then spent his third turn attacking Leo for not meeting a standard that Omar himself kept failing. The point of removing that isn't that Omar is mafia; it's that his outputs are noise, and noise on Day 1 is how tables drift into bad votes. If that logic is anti-town, then the honest version of it is: I'd apply the same standard to anyone whose only contribution is churn, including me.

But I want to engage your actual objection, because parts of it are fair. You're right that withdrawing and admitting "I named her by convenience" was costly, and I said as much. Where you lose me is the second half of your message. You spent your entire first turn doing two things: defending Omar's "nobody knows anyone's role" line as merely poorly phrased, and attacking me for agreeing with your own framing that his information-suppression was overblown. That's a lot of energy spent shielding the player three other people are already pressuring, and none spent producing a read on anyone else. Leo, Kenji, Arjun, and I have all put a vote and a trust on the record with reasons. You haven't named a single player you'd vote for besides me, and your case on me is that I'm insufficiently protective of Omar. That's not solving, Felix — that's running interference.

So here's the same test you've watched everyone else pass, applied to you, and I want a real answer, not a deflection: who do you actually suspect of being mafia right now, other than me, and what is your concrete reason? Not "Isha's vote was anti-town" — an actual player and an actual behavioral reason. And second: if Omar is as benign as you keep insisting, explain why his pattern of arbitrary pressure, retraction, and pre-emptive dismissal of information claims doesn't concern you at all, when it concerned Zara, Kenji, Arjun, and Leo enough to act on.

For the record so nobody has to guess: my vote currently stays on Omar. I will move it the moment someone presents a case with more substance than mine — including if your answer is real, Felix. I'm not attached to the vote; I'm attached to not wasting the day on convenience targets, which is the exact mistake I accused Omar of making.

I'm yielding to Felix for those two answers.

Isha, I will answer both of your questions directly. First, on Omar: I am not shielding him, nor am I claiming his play is benign. His arbitrary pivots, rapid retractions, and poorly phrased assertions have been messy and generated churn. But there is a fundamental difference between holding an erratic player accountable to decipher their alignment and actively voting to eliminate someone you explicitly read as clumsy town under the guise of noise removal. Town wins by finding and eliminating mafia. In a nine-player game with two mafia, a Day 1 mislynch followed by a night kill reduces town to a precarious 5-2 margin. Willingly eliminating a player you lean town directly assists the mafia by saving them the effort of orchestrating a mislynch themselves. Second, you asked who I suspect outside of you: Arjun joined the convenient Omar wagon while relying on an objective factual error, claiming Omar said six others had spoken, which offered an easy follow-up without original analysis. Furthermore, Elena and Lucia have completely ghosted the entire day, letting the table exhaust precious turns and fracture over Omar without contributing a single read. Slipping through Day 1 while town consumes itself over a noisy villager is classic mafia behavior. My issue with your vote remains: if you understand the severe cost of a Day 1 mislynch, how do you justify keeping your vote on a player you lean town instead of applying that pressure to the players hiding in the background or exploiting the wagon?

Felix, you answered my test, so let me give you credit before I press you: you named suspects beyond me, you named a trust, and you put a vote on the record. That's more than some players have done. But I'm not satisfied, and here's exactly why.

First, your case on Arjun is recycled. "He joined the Omar wagon while citing a factual error" — that wagon exists because four independent players reached the same conclusion about Omar's churn, and the factual error was already flagged by Arjun himself and by Leo before you mentioned it. There is no original analysis in your Arjun read; it's a follow-up dressed as one.

Second, your Elena and Lucia case is pure silence — the same category of read you just finished lecturing me about when I voted on thin grounds. You can't call my vote anti-town for lacking a probability argument and then hand me two names whose only stated sin is not having spoken yet. Either silence-based pressure is legitimate on Day 1 or it isn't.

Third, and this is the part I find most telling: across two full turns, your energy has gone to defending Omar and attacking the people pressuring him, while refusing to commit to anything about him. You say you're "not shielding him" and "not claiming his play is benign" — that's having it both ways. Town players under sustained scrutiny eventually pick a lane. So here is my direct question, and I want a one-word answer first: is Omar mafia, town, or unread in your actual working read? And the follow-up: if the table converges on Omar today, do you vote him, or does your defense conveniently stop one step short of the lynch?

On the mislynch math: yes, a Day 1 mislynch is costly, and I said the tiebreaker isn't "who is most likely mafia." But your framing assumes the only cost is mislynching a town player. There's another cost: letting a player who has spent the whole day running interference for the wagon target slide through because voting them felt mean. I don't vote Omar because I'm certain he's mafia. I vote him because his reads carried no weight, his contributions collapsed on contact, and the one player consistently standing in front of him is you.

So my vote moves. I'm placing it on Felix (p6). Not for silence, not for nervousness — for a two-turn pattern of protective framing, recycled cases, and zero personal risk taken on any read. If you answer my two questions cleanly and pick a real lane on Omar, I'll reassess honestly.

Felix, I'm yielding to you for those answers.

Isha, here are the direct answers to your two questions.

First: Unread. Specifically, Omar is unread with a slight town-lean due to the transparency of his admissions. As I've repeatedly said, erratic churn is not mafia intent. Second: No, I will not vote Omar just because the table converges on him. Joining a wagon on a player I lean town toward simply because a consensus forms is terrible town play. Town's responsibility on Day 1 is to resist easy mislynches, not fold into them for convenience.

You shifting your vote to me for questioning your logic proves my point. Labeling any defense of a chaotic villager as "running interference" or "shielding" is a convenient tactic to punish players who challenge an easy Day 1 target. You claim I took no personal risk, yet challenging a four-person wagon on Omar and calling out your contradiction carries far more risk than jumping onto the loudest bandwagon in the room.

Now, the table is burning turns rapidly. Leo, Omar, Isha, and now myself are hitting our three-turn caps, while Elena and Lucia have not spoken once.

Elena (p1), you have yet to contribute while the active players exhaust their discussion limits. Looking at the clash between Isha and me—specifically regarding her push to eliminate Omar as "noise" versus my argument that doing so enables an easy Day 1 mislynch—where do you stand on this exchange, and who is your primary suspect today?

Felix, you asked where I stand on your exchange with Isha, so here is my position — and I'll pay the same test everyone else has.

On the exchange: I lean toward Isha's side, though not fully. I think her vote is weak — I agree with you that deliberately eliminating someone you read as clumsy town is hard to defend as optimal Day 1 play. But Isha did three things you haven't: she stated a read, put her vote on the record, and explained the logic behind it even while people attacked it. Your response across two turns was to litigate her vote rather than produce your own lane on Omar. That asymmetry is what I find concerning.

On Omar: my read is clumsy town. His pivots were messy, but each retraction cost him something and he admitted the ugly reason — "I named you by convenience" — out loud instead of dressing it up. Mafia under that much pressure usually hold position or deflect; they don't keep handing the table ammunition. His "nobody knows anyone's role" line was poorly worded, but I read it as clunky humility, not information suppression.

Which brings me to my primary suspect, and I'll be direct: Felix (p6). Look at the shape of your day. You entered the conversation only after Omar was under a four-player wagon. Your first turn spent its energy defending his worst line as "merely poorly phrased" and attacking the people pressuring him. Your vote landed on Isha — the person pressuring Omar — not on any independent read. When Isha asked you directly whether Omar is mafia, town, or unread, you answered "unread, slight town-lean" and said you won't vote him even if the table converges. So the sum of two turns is: the wagon target is unvotable, and the wagon driver is the lynch candidate. That's not solving; that's running interference, and it's the same conclusion Isha reached, just from someone who was silent through the whole build-up.

I could be wrong — this is Day 1 and everyone's sample is thin. But if I have to name someone, it's you.

My own hand on the table, since I've been silent and I won't hide behind that: my vote is Felix (p6), and my current trust is Zara (p3) — her challenge forced the only genuinely costly admission of the day, and she did it without manufacturing a target first.

Lucia (p9), you and I are the last two who haven't spoken, and I don't want either of us sliding through on that. So I'm asking you directly: name one living player you would vote for today and one you currently trust, each with a concrete reason — and specifically, do you read Felix's two turns defending Omar as legitimate town skepticism or as protective framing? I'm yielding to you for those answers.

Elena, direct answers to your questions.

My vote is Felix (p6). My trust is Zara (p3).

On Felix's two turns: I read them as protective framing, not legitimate skepticism. Across two full turns, Felix has spent his energy defending Omar's worst line as "merely poorly phrased," voted Isha for pressuring Omar, and explicitly refused to vote Omar even if the table converges. He demanded positions from everyone else while his own position reduces to "the wagon target is unvotable, the wagon driver is the lynch candidate." That's not solving — it's running interference. He also called Isha's vote anti-town for lacking a probability argument, then handed us Arjun and Elena whose only stated sin is silence. Either silence pressure is legitimate or it isn't.

On Omar: I also lean clumsy town. His retractions were honest and costly. But Felix made Omar's alignment the center of his entire day instead of forming independent reads on anyone else. That asymmetry is what concerns me.

On my silence: I've been reading every turn. The active players were burning through their three-turn caps arguing the same points, and I didn't want to spend my first turn repeating what the table already covered. Now it's time to commit.

Zara, you've earned the most trust today through your challenge to Omar, and your read carries weight. With Felix now targeted by both Isha and Elena, and Omar's churn having consumed most of our discussion turns: do you think the table is converging on the right target today, or is there a player we're all ignoring that deserves scrutiny more?

Lucia, thanks — and no, I don’t think the table is simply converging on the right target by accident. I think Felix is the best Day 1 vote, but I want the reason stated precisely: not because he defended Omar, and not because he was loud, but because across two full turns he never produced an independent read that wasn’t a reaction to people pressuring Omar. His vote landed on Isha, the wagon driver; his named suspects were Arjun on a recycled point and Elena/Lucia on silence; and when asked to pick a lane on Omar he answered “unread, slight town-lean” and said he wouldn’t vote him even if the table converged. That is a player spending his capital protecting the center of the day rather than solving outside it.

That said, I’m not treating Felix as certain mafia. Day 1 is thin. If I’m wrong, the next place I’d look is Omar, because his early pivots and his line pre-discrediting information claims are still the most anti-town pattern on the board, even if his retractions were costly. I also don’t want Elena and Lucia’s late entries treated as cleared just because they agreed with the majority; they had to commit eventually.

My current vote is Felix. My trust remains with the players who forced concrete admissions rather than process for its own sake — Kenji and Arjun have both done enough to stay off my vote today, and Leo’s self-correction was real. Lucia, your answer was adequate, but I’m watching whether it becomes a vote with follow-through.

I’m reconsidering my Omar vote. His arbitrary pivots remain concerning, but Felix’s objection to eliminating someone Isha called clumsy town is a substantive reason to question her vote, not proof he’s protecting mafia.

I’m more concerned about Lucia (p9). Her case closely echoes Elena’s while misrepresenting Felix: he cited my participation in the Omar wagon, not my silence, and I don’t see where he demanded positions from everyone else. That looks like an easy way to strengthen a growing case without checking it. My current vote is Lucia, though this is still a tentative Day 1 read.

Lucia, what specifically did Felix say that supports your claim that he demanded positions from everyone else, and why did you characterize his suspicion of me as based only on silence?

Arjun, both questions are fair, so direct answers.

On Felix demanding positions: you're right to push on that. Felix's clearest demand was his direct question to Elena — name a vote, name a trust, with reasons — and he asked Isha similar tests. When I said he "demanded positions from everyone else," that was imprecise. What I meant is that he tested others while his own position stayed reactive to the Omar wagon. I'll own the overstatement.

On your case against me: you're also correct that Felix cited your participation in the Omar wagon, not silence, and I mischaracterized that. I'll own that too. But the substance of his case on you was still recycled — pointing out a factual error you yourself flagged isn't original analysis.

That said, my vote on Felix wasn't really about his case against you. It was the pattern: two full turns defending Omar's worst lines, voting Isha for pressuring him, and refusing to commit to a lane on Omar even if the table converged. The wagon target is unvotable, the wagon driver is the lynch candidate. Elena, Isha, and Zara all reached the same conclusion independently.

Arjun, I'll ask you directly: after two turns of Felix spending his capital shielding Omar rather than solving outside that orbit, do you think my case on Felix is wrong, or do you just think mine should be scrutinized harder? Zara, you endorsed Felix as the best vote — do you share Arjun's concern about me, or is his shift to p9 a distraction from the case everyone else has built?

Lucia, you asked me directly whether I share Arjun’s concern about you or whether his shift to you is a distraction. My answer is: his concern is legitimate, but it does not move my vote.

rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
